strengths: Clear motivation grounded in cognitive science literature (Flower & Hayes, Polya, Flavell) drawing a meaningful analogy between human iterative problem-solving and proposed RL training
Concrete and well-scoped method: iGRPO is a minimal, targeted extension of GRPO with a clear two-stage mechanism that is easy to understand
Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, MATH500, AMC23, GSM8K, Minerva) with multiple base models and parameter scales, culminating in state-of-the-art numbers
Efficiency-conscious design that reuses existing group reward signals, reducing overhead concerns
weaknesses: The core idea—feeding the best-of-N draft back as a prompt prefix—is relatively simple and may lack sufficient technical novelty to distinguish from existing best-of-N sampling or iterative self-refinement methods (e.g., Self-Refine, Reflexion)
No ablation or analysis on why the highest-scoring draft (vs. random or average) serves as the best self-feedback signal; the design choice is stated but not justified empirically within the intro
Generalization beyond mathematical reasoning is not addressed; the framing implies broad applicability but all experiments are math-specific

The gap identification ('RL algorithms do not incorporate feedback') glosses over a rich literature on iterative RL, online RLHF, and multi-turn RL that partially addresses this gap—no serious engagement with these works in the intro

ai_detection.reasoning: The introduction follows a highly formulaic three-part structure (prior work → gap → proposed method → experiments), uses standard transitional phrases ('Yet, in the realm of...', 'In this work, we propose'), and presents exactly the canonical three-bullet-style contribution summary compressed into a single paragraph. The cognitive science citation cluster feels decorative rather than deeply integrated. Prose is competent but uniform in rhythm and lacks the varied sentence structure and discursive texture typical of human-written academic introductions.
